en: We test "what if" questions about people and society with AI-designed simulations. Change the variables and run them yourself.
Is success luck? How do rumors spread? We test "what if" questions about people, society, nature and art with simulations, and publish them so you can change the variables and run them yourself.
Play with the dots. They dodge your cursor, and a click asks "what if?": they scatter, then sort themselves out again.
28 experiments in 10 fields (columns). Hover a cell and its page opens in the lab notebook below.
Talent clusters around the average, so why does wealth pile up in a few hands? Is the richest person really the most talented?
Even if every trade is as fair as a coin flip, does wealth concentrate? How much sharing does it take to stop it?
Why Do Only the Top 1% of YouTubers Break Through?
Does good content win, or do channels that broke out first keep winning? Compare parallel universes that start with the same channels.
Why Birds of a Feather Flock Together
Can a mild wish like "I don't want to be a minority" split a neighborhood completely apart?
How fast does a rumor spread, and through whom? How late can a correction come and still matter?
Does Lowering Your Standards Help You Find a Match?
See how aspiration level affects the time to find a partner in a market where both sides must agree.
Does promoting your best performers make an organization better? Compare promotion methods.
Does the Voting Method Change the Winner?
Count the same votes by plurality, runoff, ranked-choice and Borda. Can the winner change?
Phantom Traffic Jams: Why Does Traffic Stop Without an Accident?
Watch how a single occasional tap of the brake can block a whole road.
Why Is the Popular Restaurant Always Packed?
Why does everyone lose when everyone thinks alike? And what if predictions differ?
Test the idea that order isn't kept by itself but by someone paying a price to keep it.
Why Do Fireflies Flash in Unison?
Watch hundreds of fireflies fall into the same rhythm with no conductor.
How Does a Zebra Get Its Stripes?
Two simple reacting chemicals can form spots, stripes and mazes by themselves. Drop your own seeds.
When everyone has a different "I'll join if this many others do" threshold, can one person change the whole square?
Forest and people grow together, then crash: trace the overshoot-and-collapse curve. (The real history is still debated.)
How Does a Single Shot Become a World War?
How far does a small clash spread as alliances get denser? A cascade experiment with anonymous states.
In a world full of defectors, how do cooperation and trust come back? What changes when mistakes creep in?
Which Society Would You Choose Behind the Veil of Ignorance?
If you didn't know who you'd be, which society would you pick? The choice flips with how much you dislike risk.
Is the Tragedy of the Commons Inevitable?
Is a shared pasture doomed, or can monitoring and rules save it? Run both views side by side.
Compare monkeys typing at random with evolution that keeps the best at every step.
Why Are a Few Words Used Constantly?
Why do a few words make up most of any text? Generate one yourself with a rich-get-richer rule.
How Do Stories Change as They're Retold?
What survives as a story passes mouth to mouth? Watch only the memorable parts remain.
On a color wheel, watch the cycle created by a copying crowd and trendsetters running away.
What If 100 AI Painters Copy Each Other?
Does imitation collapse styles into one? Watch 100 paintings change.
Why Do Sunflower Seeds Sit at That Angle?
Turn each seed by 137.5° and they pack with no gaps. Nudge the angle and watch the pattern fall apart.
Why Does Winning an Auction Cost You?
The highest bidder wins, so why does the winner lose on average? How much should you shade your bid to break even?
